title: When must a company appoint a dangerous goods safety adviser under ADR?
description: ADR 1.8.3 explained: which undertakings must appoint a DGSA, the adviser's duties and annual report, the examination and the five year certificate renewal.
shortAnswer: Under ADR 1.8.3, applied in the EU by Directive 2008/68/EC, every undertaking that consigns or carries dangerous goods by road, or packs, loads, fills or unloads them, must appoint at least one dangerous goods safety adviser (DGSA), unless a national exemption applies. The adviser must hold a vocational training certificate gained by training and an approved examination. The certificate is valid for five years and is extended by passing a further examination in the year before expiry.
keyTakeaways: ADR 1.8.3.1 requires each undertaking whose activities include consigning, carrying, packing, loading, filling or unloading dangerous goods by road to appoint one or more safety advisers.
Competent authorities may exempt undertakings handling only quantities within the 1.1.3.6 and related thresholds, or occasional low risk national activity outside their main business (1.8.3.2).
The adviser monitors compliance, advises the undertaking, and prepares an annual report that must be kept for five years (1.8.3.3), plus an accident report after qualifying incidents (1.8.3.6).
The initial examination is a written test of at least 20 open questions plus a case study, set by an examining body that may not be a training provider (1.8.3.10 and 1.8.3.12).
The certificate is valid for five years and is extended for five years at a time by passing an examination in the year before expiry, without the case study (1.8.3.16).
jurisdiction: International (UNECE ADR); applied in the European Union to national and cross-border road transport by Directive 2008/68/EC
regulator: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) Working Party on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (WP.15), with each Contracting Party's competent authority designating examining bodies and issuing certificates
appliesTo: Consignors of dangerous goods by road
Undertakings that pack, load, fill or unload dangerous goods for road transport
Individuals acting as internal or external safety advisers

sections.heading: Which undertakings must appoint a safety adviser?

blocks.text: Any undertaking whose activities include consigning or carrying dangerous goods by road, or the related packing, loading, filling or unloading, must appoint one or more safety advisers. ADR 1.8.3.1 in the [2025 edition of ADR, Volume I](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2025-01/2412006_E_ECE_TRANS_352_Vol.I_WEB_0.pdf) describes the adviser as "responsible for helping to prevent the risks inherent in such activities with regard to persons, property and the environment."

In the EU, [Directive 2008/68/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02008L0068-20260512) on the inland transport of dangerous goods applies Annexes A and B of ADR, as applicable from 1 January 2025, to road transport within and between Member States. The DGSA rule therefore applies to purely domestic EU operations as well as international ones.
Under 1.8.3.2, competent authorities may choose not to apply the requirement to undertakings:

items: whose activities concern quantities in each transport unit not exceeding those in 1.1.3.6, 1.7.1.4 and Chapters 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 (small load, Class 7 excepted package, special provision, limited quantity and excepted quantity thresholds); or

whose main or secondary activities are not dangerous goods consignment, carriage or handling, but which occasionally engage in national consignment, carriage or handling of dangerous goods posing little danger or risk of pollution.

blocks.text: These are options for each Contracting Party, not automatic exemptions. A company relying on one needs evidence of the national provision and of how its own volumes stay within it.

sections.heading: What are the safety adviser's duties?

blocks.text: The adviser's main task is, under the responsibility of the head of the undertaking, to help the undertaking carry out its dangerous goods activities in accordance with the requirements and in the safest possible way (1.8.3.3). Three duties are stated as core:

items: monitoring compliance with the requirements governing the carriage of dangerous goods;
advising the undertaking on the carriage of dangerous goods;

preparing an annual report to management or a local public authority, as appropriate, on the undertaking's dangerous goods activities. Annual reports must be preserved for five years and made available to national authorities on request.

blocks.text: The adviser must also monitor a list of practices and procedures, including identification of goods, equipment checks, emergency procedures, investigation of serious accidents and infringements, use of subcontractors, verification that employees have detailed operating procedures, awareness measures, document and safety equipment checks, packing, filling, loading and unloading checks, and the existence of the security plan in 1.10.3.2. Two items concern training directly: "the proper training of the undertaking's employees, including on the changes to the regulations, and the maintenance of records of such training".

After any accident during carriage, packing, filling, loading or unloading that affects persons, property or the environment, the adviser must prepare an accident report to management or the local public authority after collecting all relevant information (1.8.3.6). Separately, 1.8.5.1 requires a report to the competent authority of a serious occurrence no later than one month after it happened.

blocks.title: Who can be the adviser
blocks.text: ADR 1.8.3.4 allows the adviser to be the head of the undertaking, an employee with other duties, or a person not directly employed by the undertaking, provided that person can perform the duties. On request, the undertaking must tell the competent authority who its adviser is (1.8.3.5).

sections.heading: How does a person qualify as a DGSA?

blocks.text: A safety adviser must hold a vocational training certificate valid for road transport, issued by the competent authority or a designated body (1.8.3.7). To obtain it, a candidate must undergo training and pass an examination approved by the competent authority (1.8.3.8).

items: **Independent examining body (1.8.3.10):** examinations are organized by the competent authority or a body it designates in writing. "The examining body shall not be a training provider", and designation depends on competence, impartiality and independence from anyone employing safety advisers.

**Subjects (1.8.3.11):** consequences and causes of accidents, then national and international requirements on classification, packing and tanks, marking and placarding, transport documents, consignment methods, mixed loading and segregation, quantity limits, handling and stowage, cleaning and degassing, crew training, vehicle documents, instructions in writing, parking supervision, traffic restrictions, pollutant discharges and transport equipment.
**Written test (1.8.3.12.4(a)):** at least 20 open questions covering the 1.8.3.11 subjects; multiple choice may be used, with two multiple choice questions counting as one open question.
**Case study (1.8.3.12.4(b)):** a case study in keeping with the 1.8.3.3 duties, to show the candidate can perform the adviser role.

**Exam conditions (1.8.3.12):** invigilated, authentication of the candidate, only international or national regulations allowed as documentation, and records kept. Electronic exams are permitted under conditions in 1.8.3.12.5.

**Restricted certificates (1.8.3.13):** Contracting Parties may allow examinations limited to Class 1, Class 2, Class 7, the group of Classes 3, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1, 5.2, 6.1, 6.2, 8 and 9, or certain fuels (UN 1202, 1203, 1223, 3475 and aviation fuel under UN 1268 or 1863). The certificate must state the restriction.

sections.heading: How long is a DGSA certificate valid and how is it renewed?

blocks.text: The certificate is valid for five years. Under 1.8.3.16.1 its validity "shall be extended from the date of its expiry for five years at a time where, during the year before its expiry, its holder has passed an examination" approved by the competent authority.

The renewal examination tests the knowledge in 1.8.3.11(b) and must include amendments to the regulations introduced since the last certificate was awarded. It is run on the same basis as the initial exam, but holders need not undertake the case study (1.8.3.16.2). If an adviser extends the scope of a certificate during its validity, the new certificate keeps the original expiry date (1.8.3.19).

Unlike the driver certificate under Chapter 8.2, ADR does not require a refresher course before the DGSA renewal examination; it requires a pass. In practice, the amendments since the last certificate become the core of preparation, which makes edition by edition change tracking the useful input for the adviser's own [refresh cycle](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

blocks.title: Multimodal certificate form
blocks.text: The model certificate in 1.8.3.18 has tick boxes for road, rail and inland waterway, and 1.8.3.15 requires all Contracting Parties to recognize certificates in that form. The ADR text itself governs the road entry.

sections.heading: How can an undertaking map DGSA obligations to evidence?

blocks.text: The table below is an original mapping of ADR 1.8.3 obligations to the responsible role, frequency and the evidence a competent authority would expect at inspection. It complements guidance on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

blocks.text: The training records the adviser monitors are the ones described on the [ADR driver training certificate](/regulations/adr-dangerous-goods-driver-training-certificate) page, so the two obligations are best managed from one [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).

sections.heading: Which version of ADR applies as at November 2026?

blocks.text: As at November 2026, the 2025 edition of ADR, applicable from 1 January 2025, is the version referenced by Directive 2008/68/EC in its consolidated text of 12 May 2026. The 2023 edition could be used only until 30 June 2025 under the transitional measure in 1.6.1.1.

Because DGSA renewal examinations must cover amendments since the last certificate, an adviser certified under an earlier edition should expect the 2025 changes to be examinable. Competent authorities publish the examining bodies and procedures for their country, and 1.8.4 requires Contracting Parties to notify UNECE of the authorities competent to implement ADR.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures the 1.8.3.11 subject list as a defined framework, with each ADR amendment tagged to the knowledge points it changes. That gives an adviser a precise list of what changed since their last certificate and gives the undertaking traceable evidence that employee training was updated when the regulations changed.

faqs.q: Can one person act as safety adviser for several companies?
faqs.a: Yes, ADR permits it. Under 1.8.3.4 the adviser may be a person not directly employed by the undertaking, provided that person is capable of performing the duties. Each undertaking keeps its own appointment obligation, annual report and accident reporting, so an external adviser serving several clients needs separate records for each.

faqs.q: Does a DGSA need to attend a refresher course every five years?
faqs.a: ADR 1.8.3.16 requires the holder to pass an examination approved by the competent authority during the year before expiry, covering amendments since the last certificate. It does not mandate a refresher course, although most candidates prepare through one. National rules may add requirements.

faqs.q: Can a training provider also run the DGSA examination?
faqs.a: No. ADR 1.8.3.10 states that the examining body shall not be a training provider. It must be designated in writing on criteria including competence, impartiality and independence from any natural or legal person employing safety advisers.

faqs.q: What happens if the annual report is not kept?
faqs.a: ADR 1.8.3.3 requires annual reports to be preserved for five years and made available to national authorities on request. The introduction to ADR 2025 notes that "ADR itself does not prescribe any penalties" and that legal action follows domestic legislation, so the consequence of a missing report depends on national law.
